items: Three tokens, one space each, then headers
Methods are case-sensitive, uppercase by convention
`get` is not `GET` — servers must reject it
Method is the semantic verb, not the implementation
GET: the only verb an address bar issues
HEAD keeps `Content-Length` — size before download
POST: the server decides what and where
PUT: the client picks the URL, full replace
PATCH applies a patch document, partial edit
JSON Patch RFC 6902, JSON Merge Patch RFC 7386
OPTIONS asks what a resource supports
OPTIONS answers with `Allow:`, and drives CORS preflight

blocks.title: Rarely Seen, Still Spec
items: TRACE echoes the request for loopback debugging
TRACE is off everywhere — Cross-Site Tracing (XST)
CONNECT opens a TCP tunnel through a proxy
That is how HTTPS crosses an HTTP proxy

blocks.title: Not Every Verb Fits Every URL
blocks.text: 405 Method Not Allowed exists for exactly this case: the resource is real, the method is not defined for it.

items: Extension methods are legal: WebDAV `PROPFIND`, `MKCOL`, `LOCK`
Only registered methods get generic intermediary handling
Safe = read-only semantics, no intended state change
Safe set: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE
Safe is not zero side effects — logs, analytics, counters are fine
The client just isn't responsible for that change
N identical requests = same server state as 1
Idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE
It is about server state, never the response body

blocks.title: Safe Implies Idempotent
blocks.text: The reverse is false: PUT and DELETE change state, but repeating them changes nothing further.

items: GET and HEAD cacheable by default
POST only with explicit freshness headers
PUT, DELETE, PATCH: never cacheable
POST is neither safe nor idempotent
Hence the browser's Confirm Form Resubmission on reload
An append op grows the array on every call
An absolute merge patch is idempotent
Proxies and clients auto-retry idempotent requests on connection failure
Crawlers and prefetchers follow GET links freely
Never hide a destructive action behind a GET

blocks.title: `GET /posts/42/delete`
items: A prefetcher or antivirus scanner opens the link
The database is wiped and no user ever clicked
Use POST or DELETE — never a bare href

blocks.title: `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>`
items: Stripe and PayPal pattern for retryable POST
Server stores the key, replays the first response
Same key twice bills the customer once
GET must carry no semantically meaningful body
RFC 9110: a body may cause implementations to reject it
Complex queries go in the query string
Or POST to `/search` and accept losing cacheability
URL length is not spec-limited, only practically capped
~2 KB by IE legacy behaviour
~8 KB by nginx `large_client_header_buffers`
`If-Modified-Since: <date>` also yields 304
206 powers resumable downloads and video seeking

slides.page_title: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS in Depth

items: Must return exactly the headers GET would
MUST NOT return a body, ever
A server sending `Content-Length: 0` on HEAD is broken
Uses: link checkers, cache probes, size before a big download
`OPTIONS * HTTP/1.1` asks about the server, not a resource
Preflight sends `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `-Request-Headers`
Triggered by PUT, PATCH or DELETE
Or by non-simple headers: `Authorization`, custom `X-*`
Or by `Content-Type: application/json`

blocks.title: Preflight Runs Unauthenticated
blocks.text: Your OPTIONS handler must answer 200 or 204 without a token. Requiring auth on preflight breaks every browser client.

blocks.title: Never Mutate On GET
blocks.text: A convenience endpoint like `/api/refresh-cache` behind GET is a bug waiting for a crawler.

left.title: POST
items: server picks the URL
201 + `Location`
not idempotent
create, or any action

right.title: PUT
items: client picks the URL
creates or replaces
idempotent
full representation
`PUT /users/42` writes exactly at that URL
If you can't name the URL first, it's a POST
PUT is a full replacement — omitted fields are deleted
Sending `{"name":"Ada"}` wipes that user's email
PATCH changes only the described fields
JSON Patch is an ordered op array — expressive but verbose
Never send bare `application/json` on PATCH and expect interop
Declare the patch format or nothing interoperates
`PUT /users` means replace the whole collection
Almost never what anyone actually wants
RPC over HTTP loses caching, retry safety, intermediary understanding
POST is the escape hatch for non-CRUD actions
`POST /orders/8812/cancel`
`POST /jobs/9/retry`
Guard PUT/PATCH with `If-Match: "etag"`
Stale etag returns 412 Precondition Failed — no lost update
`If-None-Match: *` makes a create-only PUT

slides.page_title: DELETE, Soft Deletes and Async Work

items: `DELETE /users/42` requests removal
204 No Content when there is nothing to return
200 with a body describing what was deleted also fine
202 Accepted when the deletion is queued
On 202, return `Location` to a status resource
The client polls that URL for the outcome
Some APIs answer 204 on repeat to keep clients simple
Both are defensible — document which you chose
410 Gone asserts it existed and was intentionally removed
Search engines drop 410 URLs faster than 404
Soft delete (`deleted_at`) is business logic, not HTTP
Over the wire it should still look like DELETE
Not `POST /users/42/soft-delete`
DELETE with a body is legal but proxies drop it — never rely on it
Bulk delete has no clean HTTP shape
`DELETE /users?ids=1,2,3` is one pragmatic choice
`POST /users/bulk-delete` is the other

blocks.title: 405 Without `Allow:` Is Malformed
blocks.text: The spec says a 405 MUST list what is allowed. Most frameworks forget the header, and clients guess.

slides.page_title: DELETE, Soft Deletes and Async Work (cont.)

items: Name the blocking children in a 409 body
Return `Cache-Control: no-store` on the DELETE
A 2xx from an unsafe method invalidates that URL in shared caches
The first digit is the class
An unrecognized `418` MUST be treated as `400`
x00 is the generic fallback of every class
100 Continue: client sends `Expect: 100-continue` and waits
Saves uploading a huge body the server would reject
101 Switching Protocols: the WebSocket handshake
With `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade`
103 Early Hints ships before the real response
`Link: </style.css>; rel=preload` starts assets early
200 OK: generic success, body carries the representation
Right for GET, and for POST/PUT/PATCH returning the entity
201 Created: a new resource exists, MUST include `Location:`
202 Accepted: valid and queued, outcome not guaranteed
204 No Content: success, deliberately no body
Right for DELETE, and PUT/PATCH when the client knows the state
205 Reset Content tells the client to clear the submitted form
206 Partial Content answers a `Range` request
206 pairs with `Accept-Ranges: bytes` on the full response

blocks.title: 204 vs Empty 200
items: 204 says do not expect a body at all
200 with `Content-Length: 0` is wasteful and confuses clients
A 204 MUST NOT send a body or `Content-Length`
Servers that emit both break keep-alive parsing

blocks.title: A 200 With An Error Body Is A Lie
blocks.text: Returning 200 plus `{"error": "..."}` defeats every generic client, proxy, monitor and retry policy you will ever use.

items: 301 Moved Permanently: new canonical URL, update the links
Search engines transfer to the new URL
302 Found: temporary, and the most misused code in HTTP
The spec said 302 keeps the method
Every browser rewrote POST to GET anyway
RFC 7231 split the semantics into 303 and 307
303 See Other always switches the client to GET
307 Temporary Redirect MUST preserve method and body
308 is 301 that preserves method and body
POST stays POST across 307 and 308
PRG is why refresh does not resubmit the order
303 is the correct code for it — not 302
304 Not Modified means your cached copy is still valid
No body, and MUST include the validators such as `ETag`
Emitted for `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since`
Saves the entire payload, keeps the headers
300 Multiple Choices is effectively dead
305 Use Proxy is deprecated and a security hazard

blocks.title: Permanent Really Sticks
items: Browsers and caches remember 301/308 aggressively
A wrong permanent redirect lives in users' browsers for months
Ship 302 first, promote it once proven
HTTPS upgrade: 301 to the canonical `https://` origin
Pair it with HSTS `Strict-Transport-Security`

blocks.title: Loops Cap At ~20 Hops
blocks.text: Clients follow about 20 redirects then error. The usual cause is a trailing-slash rule your app and load balancer disagree on.

caption.text: Most APIs use about six status codes and get half of them wrong. This field manual walks every method and every status family — what safe, idempotent and cacheable actually mean, why 302 after a POST eats your form body, and the exact difference between 401 and 403, 400 and 422, 502 and 504. Ten pages of dense notes you can check a route against before you ship it.
